draft.change: Add Genesis 12:19 as an example of the existing Hebrew sense why-for-what-purpose.
draft.definition: With prefixed לְ, מָה asks for the reason for an action or state.
draft.evidence: In Genesis 12:19 Pharaoh asks why Abram said that Sarai was his sister.

analysis.evidence: Pharaoh quotes what Abram said, אֲחֹתִי הִוא, ‘She is my sister.’ לָמָה modifies אָמַרְתָּ, ‘you said’, asking why Abram said it.
analysis.morphology: The prefixed preposition לָ joins the interrogative מָה, ‘what?’. Together they ask ‘why?’
analysis.sense: Asks the reason for Abram’s statement.

analysis.evidence: Pharaoh asks Abram why he said אֲחֹתִי הִוא (“She is my sister”). The words immediately following אָמַרְתָּ quote Abram’s statement.
analysis.morphology: Qal perfect, second person masculine singular. The ending ־תָּ marks the subject “you.”

analysis.evidence: Pharaoh quotes Abram’s words אֲחֹתִי הִוא, “She is my sister,” then calls Sarai אִשְׁתְּךָ, “your wife.” The suffix refers to Abram as the speaker of the quoted words.
analysis.morphology: Feminine singular common noun in the construct state with a first-person singular possessive suffix.

analysis.evidence: Carried forward: this word and its source tagging were reviewed identically at 68626:14, 68622:10, 68108:6, 67330:14, 66582:2, 66324:6, 66316:6.
analysis.morphology: Independent third-person feminine singular pronoun, written הִוא and read הִיא.

analysis.evidence: Pharaoh says וָאֶקַּח אֹתָהּ לִי לְאִשָּׁה, “so I took her as my wife.” The phrase לִי לְאִשָּׁה specifies the marital sense.
analysis.morphology: The prefixed conjunction וָ marks the Qal wayyiqtol. The אֶ־ prefix marks first person common singular.

draft.change: Add Gen 12:19 as an example of the existing Hebrew sense le-dative.
draft.definition: לְ marks the person for whom an action is done, including the doer himself.
draft.evidence: In Gen 12:19 Pharaoh says וָאֶקַּח אֹתָהּ לִי לְאִשָּׁה, “I took her for myself as a wife.” Gen 11:29 uses the same construction in the plural when Abram and Nahor take wives לָהֶם, “for themselves.”

analysis.evidence: In וָאֶקַּח אֹתָהּ לִי לְאִשָּׁה, “I took her for myself as a wife,” אֹתָהּ identifies whom Pharaoh took, לִי identifies for whom he took her, and לְאִשָּׁה gives her role.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew preposition לְ with a first-person common singular pronominal suffix. The suffix refers to Pharaoh, also the subject of וָאֶקַּח, so English uses the reflexive “myself.”
analysis.sense: Marks the person for whom the action is performed, here the speaker himself.

analysis.evidence: Pharaoh says וָאֶקַּח אֹתָהּ לִי לְאִשָּׁה, “I took her as my wife.” His next words, הִנֵּה אִשְׁתְּךָ, “here is your wife,” confirm the marital sense.
analysis.morphology: The preposition לְ marks the role in which she was taken. אִשָּׁה is a feminine singular common noun in the absolute state.

analysis.morphology: Conjunction וְ prefixed to the adverb עַתָּה.

analysis.morphology: Hebrew demonstrative particle used as an interjection. It has no prefix or suffix. The following נָא is a separate particle.
analysis.sense: see now (a fact put before the hearer)

analysis.evidence: Pharaoh says he took her לִי לְאִשָּׁה, “as my wife,” then tells Abram הִנֵּה אִשְׁתְּךָ, “here is your wife.” The suffix identifies Abram as her husband.
analysis.morphology: Feminine singular common noun in the construct state with a second-person masculine singular possessive suffix.

analysis.evidence: Pharaoh identifies the implied object with הִנֵּה אִשְׁתְּךָ, “here is your wife.” The following command וָלֵךְ, “and go,” shows that Abram is to take her with him when he leaves.
analysis.morphology: Qal imperative, second person masculine singular, addressed to Abram. The initial ל of the root drops out. The form has no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: Pharaoh points out Abram’s wife with הִנֵּה אִשְׁתְּךָ and then says קַח וָלֵךְ, “take her and go.” The second command directs Abram to leave.
analysis.morphology: The conjunction וָ joins לֵךְ, a Qal imperative masculine singular, to the preceding imperative קַח. Both commands address Abram.
